_meta.what: Published AGGREGATE findings on how much archaeological and burial ground has already been looted or destroyed, and — where anyone has published it — how densely sites occur.
_meta.why_aggregate_only: This file holds percentages and counts that researchers have already published, at regional or national scale. It contains NO site coordinates and is never derived from a site register. Deriving a density surface ourselves would mean ingesting and holding the coordinates, and a harvester that stores a site register IS a site register no matter what it publishes. So: only figures the source itself put in print, plotted at the centroid of the area the study covered.
_meta.read_this_first: These are not comparable to each other. Different studies, methods, date ranges, definitions of 'site' and 'looted'. A figure here means one team measured one area one way and published the number. It is evidence that the problem has been quantified somewhere, not a global rate.
_meta.density_caveat: Site DENSITY figures measure survey effort at least as much as they measure sites. An area with many recorded sites is an area archaeologists have worked. Read a low density as 'nobody has surveyed here', never as 'nothing is here'.

findings.unit: percent of sites looted or damaged
findings.note: Damage classified into traditional looting, mechanised looting by bulldozer, militarisation, and construction or encampments. The authors single out mechanised looting and its association with military activity.

findings.unit: percent of sites impacted by looting
findings.compare: an order of magnitude above pre-war levels
findings.note: Frequency and severity varied significantly between areas held by different factions — looting tracked control, not just chaos.

findings.unit: percent of surveyed sites showing looting
findings.source: Parcak, Gathings, Childs, Mumford & Cline, Antiquity 90(349) (2016)
findings.note: The first systematic country-scale assessment attempted anywhere in the Middle East. Required multi-temporal imagery to tell looting pits from unbackfilled excavation trenches — the two look alike from orbit.

findings.denominator: comparison of historic maps against satellite time series
findings.period: past two centuries, majority in the last 40 years
findings.source: Parcak (2007), cited in Lasaponara et al. (2014)
findings.note: Loss here includes destruction by development and encroachment, not looting alone. The acceleration is the finding: most of two centuries of loss happened in the most recent fifth of it.

findings.unit: percent of burial mounds destroyed and plundered
findings.denominator: burials analysed by high-resolution imagery, ground-truthed
findings.source: Caspari, Institute of Archaeological Sciences, University of Bern (2018)
findings.note: The area was chosen BECAUSE researchers expected it to be intact — remote, and heavily policed. It was not. These are Iron Age steppe burial mounds containing gold and bronze, which is what draws the digging.

findings.unit: percent of field archaeologists reporting looting at or near their sites
findings.note: The closest thing to a global figure that exists, and it measures what practitioners SEE rather than what has been counted. Its value is that it rules out the idea that looting is regionally exceptional.

findings.denominator: 546 sites across 197 km2, by pedestrian survey
findings.note: A rare published density figure, and it exists only because someone walked the ground. Treat it as a measure of what thorough survey finds, not of what is unusual about this valley.

findings.unit: percent of known sites found by remote survey
findings.denominator: 12 analysts against 546 ground-surveyed sites; best performers reached 20%
findings.note: The most useful number here. Satellite survey found under a tenth of sites already known from walking the ground — so any map built from remote sensing is missing roughly 90% of what is there. Read every blank space accordingly.

The authors note that looter pits can make a site VISIBLE to satellite survey that would otherwise be invisible. Damage is what makes some sites detectable — which means remote-sensing site inventories are biased toward the sites that have already been dug into.
